query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In a non‐equilibrium, Mg‐containing lightweight high-entropy alloy, the initial homogeneous (metastable) solid solution evolves during post‐processing (e.g., controlled thermal aging) by segregation of Mg into intermetallic precipitates. This phase evolution modifies both the surface chemistry and internal microstructure such that, under high-temperature oxidation and corrosive environments, a more protective Mg-enriched oxide layer forms and microstructural refinement improves passivation, thereby changing the alloy’s corrosion and oxidation behavior relative to its initially cast state.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast non-equilibrium HEA with a homogeneous metastable solid solution (including Mg uniformly distributed alongside other alloying elements) and a density below 6 g/cm³.
generation.intervention: Thermal aging/post-processing (or controlled isothermal treatment) to promote phase separation and microstructural evolution from the metastable state.
generation.conditions: Testing performed under identical environmental conditions; high-temperature oxidation tests (e.g., 800–900 °C) and corrosion evaluations (e.g., in 0.1 M or chloride-containing solution), comparing thermally aged samples to the as-cast baseline.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates (and potential associated grain boundary/phase refinement) which serve as sites for preferential Mg segregation at the surface.
generation.mechanism: Thermal energy during post-processing enables Mg to partition out of the supersaturated BCC (or FCC) solid solution into stable intermetallic phases. This segregation alters the local chemical environment at grain boundaries and the alloy surface, promoting the formation of a thin, adherent, Mg-enriched oxide scale during high-temperature exposure. The changed oxide composition and refined interphase boundaries lower the corrosion current density and improve oxidation resistance compared to the as-cast alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast baseline, thermally aged samples will show: (1) evidence of Mg-rich intermetallic particle formation and microstructural refinement, (2) formation of a thinner, more uniform and protective Mg-enriched oxide scale after high-temperature exposure, (3) decreased corrosion current density and improved passivation behavior in corrosive media.
generation.baseline: The as-cast, metastable HEA with a uniform distribution of Mg and other elements and without significant intermetallic phase formation, showing relatively higher oxidation spallation and corrosion rate.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is relevant for lightweight HEAs with densities below 6 g/cm³ and compositions where elemental property differences (e.g., between Mg and other constituents) are sufficient to promote intermetallic formation under suitable thermal conditions; deviations in processing that preclude phase evolution may not follow this mechanism.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative extent of Mg segregation, the precise composition and protective effectiveness of the evolved oxide layer, and the interplay with other alloying elements are not fully predictable and may vary with slight compositional or process variations.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of the identical non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight HEA: one as-cast (control) and one subjected to a specified thermal aging protocol. Expose both groups to identical high-temperature oxidation (e.g., 850 °C for 100 hours) and corrosion tests in a chloride-containing solution. Conduct detailed microstructural analyses (using SEM, TEM, and XPS) to assess Mg segregation and oxide layer characteristics.
measurements: Phase identification and quantification of intermetallic precipitates via XRD and TEM.
Surface oxide composition and thickness via XPS and cross-sectional SEM.
Electrochemical measurements (potentiodynamic polarization) to compare corrosion current density and passivity behavior.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermally aged samples do not show statistically significant increases in Mg segregation into intermetallic phases and if the resulting oxide scale is not demonstrably thinner/more uniform or protective (i.e., if corrosion current density and oxidation spallation characteristics remain statistically similar to those of the as-cast control), then the proposed mechanism is falsified.

Designing TiZrNbTa-Al Medium-Entropy Alloy for Next-Generation Hydrogen Storage

Abstract: Medium-entropy alloys (MEAs) represent a promising class of materials for solid-state hydrogen storage due to their high hydrogen affinity, structural stability, and tunable properties. In this work, a compositional series of (TiZrNbTa){100−x}Alx (x = 0–10 at. %) MEAs were prepared and systematically investigated to clarify the influence of aluminum addition on microstructure, mechanical response, and hydrogen sorption behavior. The alloys were synthesized by arc melting, homogenized by annealing, and characterized using microscopy, X-ray diffraction, density measurements, microhardness testing, nanoindentation, and hydrogen absorption/desorption experiments. Hydrogen sorption was evaluated by isobaric absorption measurements at 2 MPa H2 over two consecutive cycles, complemented by thermogravimetric desorption analysis of hydrogenated samples. The results show that aluminum addition significantly affects activation behavior, hydrogen uptake, and residual hydrogen retention, while simultaneously increasing hardness and elastic modulus in a non-linear manner. Modeling and Experimental Results of Selected Lightweight Complex Concentrated Alloys, before and after Heat Treatment

Abstract: Lightweight complex concentrated alloys (LWCCA), composed of elements with low density, have become a great area of interest due to the high demand in a large number of applications. Previous research on LWCCAs was focused on high entropy multicomponent alloy systems that provide low density and high capability of solid solution formation. Present research introduces two alloy systems (Al-Cu-Si-Zn-Mg and Al-Mn-Zn-Mg-Si) that contain readily available and inexpensive starting materials and have potential for solid solution formation structures. For the selection of appropriate compositions, authors applied semi-empirical criteria and optimization software. Specialized modeling software (MatCalc) was used to determine probable alloy structures by CALPHAD, non-equilibrium solidification and kinetic simulations. The selected alloys were prepared in an induction furnace. Specimens were heat treated to provide stable structures.
